title: Double neural bypass restores arm movement and touch for Keith Thomas, paralyzed since a 2020 diving accident
summary: Keith Thomas, paralyzed since 2020, regained arm movement and touch after a 15-hour brain-implant operation in Manhasset, New York.
account: On 9 March 2023, surgeons led by Ashesh Mehta and Netanel Ben-Shalom implanted five microelectrode arrays in the brain of Keith Thomas, 45. The 15-hour operation was at North Shore University Hospital. A diving accident on 18 July 2020 had paralyzed him from the chest down. The Feinstein Institutes' double neural bypass decodes his movement intentions with recurrent neural networks and reinforcement learning. It pairs them with patterned spinal cord stimulation and restores touch by cortical microstimulation. By 28 July 2023 he could move his arms at will and feel his sister's hand. The Feinstein release of 16 July 2026 on the Nature Medicine paper reports 86% and 62% arm-strength gains, self-feeding and gains persisting beyond two years.
purpose: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03680872 describes an early feasibility trial of the Bidirectional Neural Bypass System. It is meant to restore movement and sensation in the hand and wrist of up to seven people with tetraplegia. This benefit is that purpose.
system: Double neural bypass (Bidirectional Neural Bypass System): intracortical brain-computer interface with an LSTM decoder and deep reinforcement-learning agent, patterned spinal cord stimulation and intracortical microstimulation
developer: Feinstein Institutes for Medical Research, Northwell Health (Institute of Bioelectronic Medicine, Chad Bouton)
deployer: Northwell Health, North Shore University Hospital
segment: Complete cervical spinal cord injury (C4 sensory/C5 motor tetraplegia)

ratings.reason: Thomas regained voluntary arm movement, touch in a hand insensate since 2020, self-feeding and drinking from a cup. Strength gains persisted more than two years. Life-changing for one identifiable person, not life-saving.

ai_role.statement: The AI is the decoder: recurrent neural networks (an LSTM) and a deep reinforcement-learning agent that turn motor-cortex activity into stimulation patterns. It reached up to 84.6% decoding accuracy sustained over five months without retraining (Feinstein release, 16 July 2026). Restored touch came from patterned intracortical microstimulation. The authors attribute the lasting strength gains to neuroplasticity from pairing the two. The decoder is necessary for real-time movement but is one part of a surgical, stimulation and rehabilitation package. The Nature Medicine paper does not name its participant. The Feinstein Institutes identify him as Thomas.

produced_by: Chronic complete cervical spinal cord injury (C4 sensory/C5 motor) with movement intentions still readable from motor cortex
Five microelectrode arrays placed in motor and somatosensory cortex during a 15-hour mapped operation with the participant partly awake
An LSTM plus deep reinforcement-learning decoder paired with patterned spinal cord stimulation and intracortical microstimulation
Thirty-five weeks of supervised laboratory sessions inside an approved early-feasibility trial (NCT03680872)
must_hold: Decoder accuracy sustained over months (84.6% over five months) so intended movements reliably trigger stimulation
Neurosurgical, engineering and rehabilitation teams present throughout. The gains were measured in the laboratory
Follow-up with the system switched off to confirm that strength and sensation gains persist

headline: Double neural bypass restores Keith Thomas's movement and touch

comparator.against: his own pre-stimulation (pre-tSCS) baseline volitional elbow-flexion forces
comparator.before: The patient presented with minimal ability to lift his arms off his wheelchair armrests, could not bring his hands to his face and had no volitional finger movement.
comparator.after: gains in volitional force reached up to 86% and 62% (right and left arm)
comparator.quote: Further, over a period of approximately 35 weeks since initiating tSCS, gains in volitional force reached up to 86% and 62%, respectively, compared with pre-tSCS baseline volitional forces

later.note: The Feinstein Institutes' July 2026 release on the Nature Medicine paper reports that the strength and sensation gains were still present at a follow-up more than two years later.
later.quote: “Remarkably, in a recent follow up, it was found these gains were still present after more than two years. This is incredibly encouraging,” said Dr. Bouton.
